title: Show Respect by Asking Others to Go First
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that among the many ways leaders can show respect, one of the most powerful and underused is simply insisting that others go first, speaking, deciding, or acting before the leader does. It frames listening to a team member's view before offering one's own as a distinct form of honor that validates the other person's opinion as significant on its own terms. The article lists a long string of concrete "go first" scenarios, presenting, choosing, exiting, giving feedback, arguing that each one signals the leader's confidence in the team member's value. It closes with a reciprocity argument: leaders who consistently give respect first are ultimately the ones who receive it.
points: Insisting that others go first, in speaking, deciding, or acting, is framed as an underused but powerful way to show respect.
Listening to a team member's view before sharing your own signals that their opinion is treated as genuinely significant, not just tolerated.
The tactic requires selflessness and confidence, since it means visibly ceding the floor or the first move to someone else.
The article closes on a reciprocity principle: leaders who give respect first are the ones who ultimately receive it from their teams.
quotes: Team members want a lot from their leader. They want to be heard, liked, valued, appreciated, and involved.
Savvy leaders who are acutely aware of the critical nature of respect do something less common but powerfully important to show their respect. They insist that others go first.
Listening to a team member before offering their own view is a unique sign of respect by a leader.
Letting others go first is a powerful way to demonstrate how much you appreciate and admire who they are.
Leaders who want to be heard listen to others (in many ways) first. Leaders give respect to receive it.
